_comment: Shipped to PLUGIN INSTALLS only. This repo's own dev hooks live in .claude/settings.json
and are unrelated: a contributor working in the checkout is not running the plugin.
TWO HOOKS, and the second one is an exception that has to be argued for, because this
file used to say ONE and the reasoning it gave is still correct. It read:
The repo's other two gates are NOT wired: require_commit_before_message.sh blocks a
tool call when the tree is dirty, and no-heredoc-source.sh blocks a class of Bash
command. Both are good rules and both are somebody's opinion about how their repo
should work -- installing a review harness must not silently start refusing a
stranger's commands.
That still holds, and those two are still not wired. murderboard_model_gate.sh is a
different KIND of object and the difference is the whole justification: the other two
refuse a stranger's command on the authors' preference about hygiene, and this one
refuses to spend the stranger's MONEY on a cost THE MURDERBOARD ITSELF INFLICTS. /murderboard
fans out one subagent per role -- every role runs, always; scaling to stakes changes how
they run and never which -- so there is no small murderboard, and on an expensive model a
single invocation can empty a usage window in minutes. On 2026-09-07 a run under Fable
cost the author two days of access and produced no review at all: the cost landed before
the deliverable did. A tool that can do that to someone who typed one slash command is not
being polite by staying quiet about it.
So the test is not 'is this a good rule' but 'is this OUR mess'. Dirty trees and heredocs
are the user's business. The bill for our fan-out is ours.
IT IS DEFAULT-ON AND OVERRIDABLE. MURDERBOARD_ALLOW_EXPENSIVE_MODEL=1 lets a user who has
decided to spend it proceed, and MURDERBOARD_BLOCKED_MODELS re-aims the whole policy. A
gate with no way past it gets uninstalled rather than obeyed, and then there is no gate.
IT HAS AN EXPIRY. The block is about PRICE, not about a model, and prices move --
MURDERBOARD_BLOCK_REVIEW_BY carries a date and this repo's CI goes red once it passes, so
a human re-affirms the block or removes it. It never expires by itself: an expired policy
still blocks, because a cost gate that silently switches itself off at midnight is worse
than one that nags.
--hook never touches the network: it serves a cached verdict and refreshes detached, so
session startup is never blocked on a lookup. --plugin reads the commit Claude Code
recorded for this install; with no answer it exits 2 and says nothing.
